86.t: Basie's big band breaks up in 1950
86.s: The big band folded as dance halls declined, and Basie formed a small group with Clark Terry and Serge Chaloff.
86.q: Yeah, the band broke up in 1950 because that's when the little bands began to take over. And the dance halls, they began to diminish. And people, they didn't dance anymore. It became like more of a concert thing when you played, you know. In the smaller clubs, you would just -- they would sit and…

86.t: Basie disbands the big band in 1950
86.s: Declining crowds forced Basie to break up the band after a Southern tour.
86.ch: After Basie: freelancing, JATP and Hollywood
86.q: Yeah, because the crowds began to diminish in all the dance halls. And Basie, he kept his band as long as he could and he lost a tremendous amount of money trying to hold it together until he said it’s just impossible. The little bands were taking over and the smaller night clubs were taking over.…

86.t: Playing for dancers versus concerts, and the fall of big bands
86.s: Big bands played only for dancers; small groups made concerts popular and big bands became too expensive.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: I wasn’t in the band then. When I was in the band it was all dancers, it was a dance hall. That’s when the era was good because a lot of the music that they play nowadays you can’t dance by it.

86.t: Big bands collapse; Ellington's ASCAP income; working around New York
86.s: Edison and Dance discuss why dance halls closed, how Ellington kept going, and Edison's work with Coleman Hawkins and in New York studios.
86.q: Yeah. And I just got my -- you know, I just said, if everybody else can do it, I can do it. That's been sort of my philosophy. If I start feeling sorry for myself I say, well, Willie had the same thing happen to them, whoever, and they've come out victorious so how come I can't do it, you know. If…

124.t: Hampton's changing band and the decline of big bands
124.s: Big bands were suffering as small bands like Louis Jordan's thrived and the whole scene was changing.
124.q: See, this the time that Lionel was changing a lot of people, you know. A lot of people were leaving him and he was having trouble keeping musicians with him, you know. Because --

124.s: McRae says the big bands began to lose the crowds as promoters oversold, the Depression bit and musicians tired of travel.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: And this was a great year, I'd say. One of the greatest year for music -- the big bands with music -- until then we get into the small bands.

124.t: Scarcity of recording and the rise of ballrooms
124.s: Little recording went on before the big-band cycle, which moved bands from night clubs into ballrooms and society clubs.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: When (inaudible) we got into the small bands. That didn't come later. That came later after the big band circle, you know.

227.t: The 1949 collapse of the bebop bands and Kenton's groups
227.s: They list the bands that folded in 1949, and Kenton's Innovations and later Holman-Rogers band, and the rhythm sections of pianist leaders.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: That’s right and then after Innovations he put together that real good band with Porcino, Shorty [Rogers] and Count and…

227.t: The end of the big band era
227.s: Mandel says 1949 was a good time for music but a lousy time for bands, and that Elliot's band was a high-grade pickup band.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: Yeah, it was really the end of the big band era, if it wasn’t for Basie, Ellington and some Woody bands and some Kenton bands, the big band era was over. Elliot’s band was never really a band, it just had a lot of talent in it for a while, but it was a high-grade New York pickup band. That's all it…

1.t: The big bands collapse: Louis Jordan and the small rhythm-and-blues groups
1.s: Danny explains how from 1940 Louis Jordan's amplified Tympany Five and West Coast rhythm-and-blues bands made big bands unnecessary.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: What year? It was around '50. From '40, it started falling to pieces. When Louis Jordan come out with the Tympany Five, with them little bands, down to five... He could play them big old ballrooms with the Tympany Five...

1.t: Why big bands died: sweat, race records, television, airplanes
1.s: Danny and Milt say Cab's clean sophisticated music lost ground to blues on the radio, television and expensive air travel.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: ...(?)... they're looking at. And later on, they started selling sweat. See? Sweat. Who sweat the most got the most people.

99.t: Taxes, transportation costs and the end of the big bands
99.s: A 20 percent tax on ballrooms and rising costs end the big bands, replaced by package shows.
99.ch: Last years of the band and reflections
99.q: But this is what broke the camel's back. And they had raised the tax on nightclubs and ballrooms 20 percent. Now, the Tunetown Ballroom owed a 20 percent tax. They just couldn't make it.

99.t: The end of the Jeter-Pillars band
99.s: The big unit stops after Tunetown; Pillars and Jeter sell beer and Charles takes a post office job.
99.ch: Last years of the band and reflections
99.q: Well, as a big unit, we just didn't continue. I took a few jobs, we took jobs, people would ask -- and we'd use would hire the band, and radios, or maybe ten pieces, 11 pieces, like that. But it was a hard scuffle, see. It was just a hard fight.

251.t: Young musicians have not heard real big bands
251.s: Albert says young players never heard good big bands, that his own band stopped in 1940 for lack of work, and that big bands now imitate the young.
251.q: What kind of music are we talking about? The ones that play? No, maybe the young ones, that's all they know. The thing about it is this, that these young musicians have never been exposed to real good bands. Big bands. Big bands. Big bands started this band in 1940 because of the depression that…

267.t: End of the school band and smaller jobs with Kid Sheik
267.s: The big band broke up around 1949; Ford turned to smaller groups with Sheik and the Handy Brothers, playing popular tunes that were not yet labelled Dixieland.
267.q: Yeah, we had an energetic guy and he's a good hustler and he's a good talker, if you know him. And he can, he's good at finding work. Oh, yeah. So he talked, he talked the president into using the band, if he could get to, if he listened to it. But at this time he was just coming into this and the…

846.t: Small New Orleans bands vanishing in the swing era
846.s: Few New Orleans bands were available from the late 1920s to 1945, with Celestin and a few Negro bands playing seafood places by the lake.
846.q: They didn't play at all. Yeah, they had a hell of a time, and gave, finding a band to engage. There were one or two that continued, uh, um, Celestan kept a group fairly well together, although they didn't play very often. They were available. Uh, who else besides Celestan? There were two or three…

952.t: Will the big bands come back
952.s: Pete says big bands cost too much to keep; Vegas and rock venues are the main outlets; Ellington carries on.
952.ch: Callers, Bourbon Street and big bands
952.q: Well, I think I'd like to see them come back. I really would, but... I think it's on the way. You think they really ever went? Well, I mean, to keep a band intact now, with the cost of keeping a band up of any size. It's a salary that you have to pay. And you can't find many places that will pay…

154.t: The recording ban and the decline of big bands
154.s: Bert explains how the ban let vocalists with strings take over from big bands.
154.q: We had to go along with it, but that ruined the big band business. Because then vocalists started recording with string sections, recorded in Europe, which they could do, and all of a sudden the vocalists were the big thing.

155.t: After the war: big-band era and postwar medical planning
155.s: Budd digresses on baby-boom predictions, hospital building and the growth of medical schools.
155.q: Yes, about that time. It’s when that new generation of new guys — I was interested in that. One of the things I learned in medicine, this has nothing to do with this so you may want to cut this out, but I was interested in medical politics and economics and I was on a committee from the Academy of…

318.t: Big bands in Los Angeles in the 1950s
318.s: Big bands rehearsed but made little money; Benny Carter occasionally led one.
318.q: Every now and then, let’s see, Benny Carter would put a band together to go to Japan or somewhere, or he would do some jobs.

206.s: His theories: cost, bebop, the recording strike and singers like Sinatra.
206.q: Well there are so many theories about this, the demise of the big band and everything. I think largely economic, it cost some money. And then the beboppers came along with a smaller group, and probably lower overhead, and they played such interesting things that you can’t fault it you know, but I…

853.t: Life on the road and the decline of big bands
853.s: Three hundred one-nighters were fun when young but took a toll; dance halls diminished, small bands took over, and big bands lost their leaders.
853.q: Being young as I was, I was having a ball. I loved it you know. But as you get older it takes its toll. And after the big bands sort of diminished because dance halls diminished, small bands began to thrive. You know like the John Kirby band. He’s the one—the Nat King Cole Trio — we had small…

132.s: Television, the loss of radio remotes and dance halls, the war and Petrillo ended the big band era.
132.ch: Opinions on jazz and big bands
132.q: Well Chuck Cecil runs programs, the hits of ’48 and ’49 and so on. And he always opens by talking about these dance halls and we all know where they were. There was the Palladium in L.A. where Goodman broke through. There was Glen Island Casino over here and Frank Daly’s Meadowbrook, and Boston,…

561.t: Can jazz be America's popular music again
561.s: Gitler doubts it; big bands are uneconomical, though Jimmy Heath's band at the Iridium shows interest, and he recalls 1940s Sunday jam sessions.
561.q: Looking at it right now, I don’t think so, but who knows? That was a particular time, if you’re talking about big bands, you know economically it’s not feasible. In fact if you have a sextet and you want to book it, you’re probably better off cutting it back to a quintet because you might have a…

941.t: The decline of working big bands
941.s: He saw the end of touring big bands in the 70s; only rehearsal bands remain.
941.q: Yeah. I think I saw the end of the big bands in the 70s and I didn’t even know it was happening because it didn’t seem, it just didn’t seem like it was going to happen that fast but it sure did. I guess there are some good rehearsal bands around and that’s about the size of it these days. You don’t…

209.t: Arriving at the end of the big band era; ghost bands; Ray Anthony and Sy Zentner
209.s: He reached big bands at the very end, before ghost bands and tribute bands took over. His first name band was Ray Anthony around 1951-52, then Sy Zentner.
209.ch: Ray Anthony and the big band end
209.q: Yeah, there were still some ballrooms, and this was before the era of every band was a ghost band. Every band has a ghost leader now and maybe more than one.

462.t: Why the big bands ended and how times change
462.s: LaPorta discusses swing as dance music, the postwar economics and television behind the big band collapse in 1946, and how each generation hears its own music.
462.ch: Early bands and the swing era
462.q: Well my feeling about that is that essentially the music was all in danceable tempos you know, the swing and the sweet bands and everything else, they were all playing pretty much the same kinds of tempos that people could relate to them and dance to them. As jazz started to become more of an art…

226.t: Big bands in decline in the early 1950s
226.s: Big bands struggled after the war; Basie dropped to six pieces while small groups like Shearing and Brubeck thrived on colleges.
226.ch: George Shearing and becoming a manager
226.q: That was the time when Basie finally broke up and had the six pieces, you know, because it was really rough out there for big bands. But groups like George was really hot, and Dave Brubeck, and that was the hottest things going, playing the colleges and you know, so it was really — the big band it…

545.t: The future of Down Beat and where Mandel writes
545.s: He discusses Down Beat's missed potential, a coming publisher change, other magazines he writes for and the rise of jazz books.
545.q: Oh — now you’re going to get me in trouble. I think actually DownBeat has made some changes recently that I’m not really at liberty to talk about but I think they are about to announce a change in the publisher that I think will be good for it. DownBeat is in some ways frustrating. Down Beat could…

214.t: Big bands and road work in the 1950s
214.s: Studios hired no doublers, so road bands were the path; big bands faded late in the 1950s but Maynard's still drew crowds.
214.ch: Early road bands and the Army
214.q: No because I did meet people and there were plans — you know you’d meet somebody and I’m sure you know how that is too. People say hey you know, so-and-so’s going out in two weeks. And it was mostly all road work at that time because the studios at that time weren’t really employing doublers, not…

217.t: Effect of the end of the Swing Era
217.s: Big bands faded and he worked in small groups, doing his own thing.
217.q: The only big band I worked with was with Jack Teagarden. So it used to be you know you turned the radio on and you’d hear big bands broadcasting from all over you know. But that faded out and well you did have the records to listen to. And things changed, they had smaller groups, trios, you worked…

122.t: Big bands shrink to small groups
122.s: Ellington sidemen and Basie's small group at the Champagne Supper Club; Woody Herman, Buddy Rich and Kirk in 1960 Chicago.
122.ch: Rock and roll and the decline of jazz work
122.q: Oh Jimmy Lewis, I beg your pardon, yeah Jimmy Lewis. And Basie of course and Gus Johnson. Yeah they played at the Champagne Supper Club here in San Francisco, small

448.t: The big band collapse of the late 1940s
448.s: As Wilber began working professionally the big bands fell apart for economic reasons and generational change.
448.q: Yeah, sure. Yeah, when I actually was starting to get out there professionally playing, we’re talking about 1946, ‘47, ‘48, this is when the whole big band thing fell apart, partially for economic reasons, and partially because you had a whole new generation of young people coming up and it wasn’t…

366.t: Decline of the big bands and the venues that vanished
366.s: Sol blames rock and roll and recalls closed hotels, theaters and Roseland, then describes his working groups.
366.q: Probably, maybe because of the rock & roll coming in. Who knows? I remember a lot of places that the bands used to play in, Monk, were not around anymore. There was no music at the Waldorf Astoria anymore, where Benny Goodman played, Xavier Cugat played, and there was no Roosevelt Hotel anymore…

61.t: The war, the recording ban and the cabaret tax hurt big bands
61.s: No gasoline, the recording ban and the New York cabaret tax destroyed big bands and left a void.
61.ch: Columbia LPs, jazz piano and teaching
61.q: That’s pretty true, and there was a recording ban which contributed to that in some ways too. Also, the big bands were destroyed by the fact that it was impossible to go touring, no gasoline, and the New York City tax, which I think kept on after the war, prevented people from hiring bands, because…

85.t: Returning to the United States in 1938 and the state of the band scene
85.s: He intended to form a big band and found the scene little changed, with Goodman the hot name.
85.q: Well, things hadn’t really changed that much. You know, it was just a matter of three years or a little less. But no, I can’t say that I had any great impression about great change, you know.

134.t: Race records, the show format and why the big-band era faded
134.s: He says stars leaving bands to front their own groups broke up the big bands, e.g. Pres away from Basie.
134.ch: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
134.q: They always had r-and-b, always. They were what they called race records, which was the blues cats. It didn’t seem to be that much separation in the music then, because . . .

63.t: The Musicraft band and the collapse of the band business; the 1949 band
63.s: He went out with the Musicraft band, says the band business was impossible, and calls the 1949 bop-oriented band his worst period.
63.ch: After the war: analysis and the last bands
63.q: Then I’d go out on the road. Then I went out on the road with a band. It was fine. That was that Kitty Kallen, Jerry . . .

80.t: What happened to the Saints and Sinners after ten years
80.s: After the 1969 trip the band kept going with a replacement for him but the regular club jobs dried up, and it played only occasionally.
80.q: Well yeah, finally, yes. I was around, aw, I've been away from them now three, four years, and they put somebody else in my place, but they're still going, but not steady, not Pittsburgh, Columbus, Ohio, Cleveland, and all that stuff. They're not doing that. They're doing --

614.t: Where 'Herd' came from and the Second Herd's reception
614.s: George Simon coined 'Thundering Herd'. The second band met resistance as the band business collapsed at the end of 1946.
614.ch: The Second Herd and its sidemen
614.q: And, of course, that began and was used as a way of describing our music. George Simon said he thought that the band sounded like a thundering herd. And so we just kept that as billing. And the reception to the second band was certainly not as spontaneous as the first one was. And there were some…

68.t: The big band breaks up: package tours and the rise of rock
68.s: Tate recalls the first Basie band breaking up, and says agents' bird-group packages and rock killed the big bands.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: And actually, the big band, I stayed with until, you know, the first band broke up. So they disbanded for a while. I'll tell you what happened to me. I started to tell you yesterday. Well, see, I'd never been around New York anytime except to come and play with Basie, because our band was a…

232.s: Both doubt big bands will return in their day because of costs.
232.q: I don't believe it will in our day, but as the circle turns, I think it will because--but it's a question of where are they going to work.

93.t: Scat singing replaces tap and dancers take off their taps
93.s: Green says dancers took their taps off, changed names and became characters, with scat singers like Ella Fitzgerald taking their place while big bands kept travelling.
93.ch: Split, hospital and decline of tap
93.q: Because they -- actually they took their taps off, they wouldn't actually try to write the pages anymore of the art, you see, and it just got into -- they start becoming characters, you know. Quite a few of them, you know, like -- they changed their names, you understand. They just wasn't…

94.t: Breakup of the big band and joining Sidney Bechet
94.s: With big bands failing in 1947 Moore was jobless; Sidney Bechet hired him and taught him traditional jazz.
94.q: 1947. /We were beginning to see signs of whatever you call it, the handwriting on the wall. All the bands were breaking up. It was an economic situation where big bands were getting out of style. Everybody was making small bands. So that left me

73.t: Why the band changed: bebop and the closing ballrooms
73.s: They conclude it was a transition, with bebop, better-paid sidemen, and ballrooms closing.
73.q: Yeah. Evidently it was -- it wound up that way -- with all the changes happening, and then all of a sudden they said 'let's chop it off'. Evidently, because in the '50's it was like, you know, a small group. They cut it down to a small group.

149.s: Theaters and one-nighters dwindled, so in 1950 he cut down to hotel jobs and small groups.
149.ch: Compositions, singers and the end of the big band
149.q: Well, places like theatres The Fields began to close up. The one night stands, which used to be very good weren't like they used to be. A lot of places was closed.

115.t: McShann's postwar band and managers pushing small groups
115.s: He rejoined McShann's re-formed big band after the Army, which failed over bookings and managers who pushed small bands.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: No, no, this was a big band, because I even came back to McShann's band after I came out, when he came back to New York.

473.t: Cab disbands the big band in 1952 as theater guarantees disappear
473.s: Cab broke up the band because theaters were closing and the guarantee, about $1,500 plus percentage, could not be assured for the South American tour; he went out as a single.
473.ch: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
473.q: Well, he disbanded. He says, "We can't go on any longer because we're not guaranteeing. We don't get the guarantee we used to." See, we used to get something like 1,500 guarantee with a percentage.

98.t: Decline of dancing, television and the cost of big bands
98.s: Dancing, television and disc jockeys wiped out bands, and big bands today are almost impossible to run.
98.q: I don't know. We take old things, they never come back in the form that we once knew them. They may come back in different forms, just like they asked about the big bands. The big band today is almost an impossibility to run.
